questions.heading: A Linear Program Allows Fractions, and Solves Fast Because It Does
questions.stem: For a 200-project selection, the LP with each fund variable allowed between 0 and 1 is worth $51.2M. The best whole plan found so far is worth $49.8M. What can you conclude?

options.text: No whole plan is worth more than $51.2M, since the LP allows every plan and more
options.says: Right: every whole plan is also a solution of the LP, so the LP's optimum bounds them all.

options.text: Some whole plan is worth $51.2M, since rounding the LP gives a plan
options.says: Rounding an LP solution can break the budget or lose value; the LP value need not be reachable.

options.text: The best whole plan is worth $49.8M, since the LP bound is not reachable
options.says: A better plan may exist between $49.8M and $51.2M; nothing yet proves $49.8M is best.

options.text: The best whole plan is worth at least $51.2M, since integers add value
options.says: Requiring whole numbers can only remove options, so the best plan is worth at most the LP value.

questions.heading: Constraint Programming Searches Over Logic and Integers Directly
questions.stem: A vegetation crew schedule has task intervals, rules that no two tasks on one crew overlap, and whole-day durations. Which solver fits it best?

options.text: GLOP, since it solves linear programs over continuous data
options.says: GLOP is an LP solver: it allows fractions and has no notion of intervals.

options.text: SLSQP, since it follows smooth curves over continuous data
options.says: A local NLP method suits smooth curves over amounts, not whole-day schedules.

options.text: CP-SAT, since it reasons about logic over integer data
options.says: Right: scheduling with intervals and dense logic on integer data is where CP-SAT is strongest.

options.text: PDLP, since it solves very large programs over continuous data
options.says: PDLP is also an LP method; size is not the issue here, the logic is.

questions.heading: A Nonlinear Program Has Curves, and Curves Cost You Guarantees
questions.stem: A program's value grows with the square of its spend, so each extra dollar buys more than the one before. You maximize total value with a local NLP method. What is the risk?

options.text: It may stop at a point that breaks the budget, since curves ignore constraints
options.says: A constrained NLP method keeps the budget; the problem is which optimum it finds.

options.text: It will find the best split, since any local optimum of a curve is global
options.says: That holds for a concave value curve, as in the lesson, not for this one.

options.text: It will find the best split, since squares are smooth and easy to solve
options.says: Smoothness helps a local method move, not find the global optimum.

options.text: It may stop at a point that is best only nearby, since the curve bends the wrong way
options.says: Right: maximizing a convex curve has several local optima at the corners; a local method can stop at the wrong one.
